subject: math
title: Inequalities: Write, Solve and Graph x > c and x < c
seo_title: Grade 6 Inequalities Worksheets: Write Inequalities, Find Solutions and Graph on a Number Line
standard_text: Write an inequality of the form x > c or x < c to represent a constraint or condition in a real-world or mathematical problem. Recognize that inequalities of the form x > c or x < c have infinitely many solutions; represent solutions of such inequalities on number line diagrams.
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 inequalities worksheets: read and write inequalities with >, <, ≥ and ≤, test solutions, graph them on a number line with open and closed circles, and turn words like “at least” and “at most” into inequalities. 100 practice questions with answer key.
key_big: x > c has infinitely many solutions. Open circle for > and <, closed circle for ≥ and ≤.
key_sub: “At least 5” is x ≥ 5 and “at most 5” is x ≤ 5. 7 is not a solution of x > 7, because 7 > 7 is false.
body_html:
What is an inequality?

An inequality compares two amounts that may not be equal. It uses one of four symbols. Read it from left to right.

SymbolRead it asExample
>is greater thanx > 4: x is greater than 4
<is less thanx < 4: x is less than 4
≥is greater than or equal tox ≥ 4: x is 4 or more
≤is less than or equal tox ≤ 4: x is 4 or less

The open side of > or < faces the greater amount. 6 < x means the same as x > 6.

Solutions

A solution is a value of the variable that makes the inequality true. x > 7 has infinitely many solutions: 8, 7.5, 7.01, 100 and every other number greater than 7. But 7 itself is not a solution, because 7 > 7 is false.

Example

Which of these are solutions of x ≥ 6? 5, 6, 6.5, 9

Test each one. 5 ≥ 6 is false. 6 ≥ 6 is true, because ≥ includes equal. 6.5 ≥ 6 and 9 ≥ 6 are true.

Answer: 6, 6.5 and 9

Graph on a number line

Draw a circle at the number. Then shade the side with the solutions and draw an arrow, because the solutions go on forever.

SymbolCircleArrow
>open (not included)right
≥closed, filled in (included)right
<open (not included)left
≤closed, filled in (included)left

Write an inequality from words

WordsSymbolExample
more than, greater than, over, above>more than 10 people: p > 10
less than, fewer than, under, below<under 12 years old: a < 12
at least, no less than, minimum, or more≥at least 48 inches tall: h ≥ 48
at most, no more than, maximum, or less≤no more than $20: c ≤ 20
Example

An elevator holds at most 12 people. Write an inequality and list the solutions.

“At most 12” means 12 or fewer, so p ≤ 12. People come in whole numbers, so the solutions that make sense are 0, 1, 2, … , 12.

Answer: p ≤ 12

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Using a closed circle for > or <Closed circles are only for ≥ and ≤
Pointing the arrow the wrong way for x < 3< means lesser numbers, so the arrow points left
Writing “at least 5” as x < 5“At least 5” means 5 or more: x ≥ 5
Saying 7 is a solution of x > 77 > 7 is false. Only numbers greater than 7 work
Reading x < 3 as “3 is less than x”Read left to right: x is less than 3
Thinking x > 3 has only the solutions 4, 5, 6, …Decimals and fractions like 3.5 work too: infinitely many

faq.q: How do you write an inequality in 6th grade?
faq.a: Choose a letter for the unknown and find the key words. “More than” is >, “less than” is <, “at least” is ≥ and “at most” is ≤. For example, “you must be at least 48 inches tall” is h ≥ 48.

faq.q: When do you use an open circle or a closed circle on a number line?
faq.a: Use an open circle for > and <, because the number itself is not a solution. Use a closed (filled-in) circle for ≥ and ≤, because the number is included.

faq.q: Why does x > 5 have infinitely many solutions?
faq.a: Every number greater than 5 makes it true, including decimals and fractions like 5.1 and 5 1/2. The numbers never end, so there are infinitely many solutions.

faq.q: Does “at least” mean greater than or less than?
faq.a: “At least” means greater than or equal to (≥). “At least 10” means 10 or more, so 10 is included. “At most” means less than or equal to (≤).

items.q: Which inequality means the same as 22 < w?
items.e: 22 < w says “22 is less than w.” Turn it around: w is greater than 22, so w > 22. The symbol still opens toward the greater side.

items.q: What does z ≤ 16 mean?
c: z is less than or equal to 16
z is greater than or equal to 16
items.e: Read from left to right: z is less than or equal to 16. The line under the symbol means “or equal to,” so z can also be 16.

items.q: What does r > 32 mean?
c: r is greater than or equal to 32
r is less than or equal to 32
items.e: Read from left to right: r is greater than 32. The symbol opens toward r, the greater side.

items.q: Which inequality means “r is less than 36”?
items.e: “r is less than 36” is written r < 36, with r first. 36 < r says “36 is less than r,” which is the opposite.

items.q: Which sentence means the same as 24 ≤ m?
c: m is greater than or equal to 24
m is less than or equal to 24
items.e: 24 ≤ m is read “24 is less than or equal to m.” That means m is greater than or equal to 24.

items.q: Which inequality means “m is less than or equal to 30”?
items.e: “m is less than or equal to 30” is written m ≤ 30, with m first. 30 ≤ m says “30 is less than or equal to m,” which is the opposite.

items.q: Which inequality means “n is less than 38”?
items.e: “n is less than 38” is written n < 38, with n first. 38 < n says “38 is less than n,” which is the opposite.

items.q: Which inequality means the same as 39 > z?
items.e: 39 > z says “39 is greater than z.” Turn it around: z is less than 39, so z < 39. The symbol still opens toward the greater side.

items.q: Which inequality means the same as 14 ≤ y?
items.e: 14 ≤ y says “14 is less than or equal to y.” Turn it around: y is greater than or equal to 14, so y ≥ 14. The symbol still opens toward the greater side.

items.q: What does w ≥ 12 mean?
c: w is less than or equal to 12
w is greater than or equal to 12
items.e: Read from left to right: w is greater than or equal to 12. The line under the symbol means “or equal to,” so w can also be 12.

items.q: What does p < 5 mean?
c: p is greater than or equal to 5
p is less than or equal to 5
items.e: Read from left to right: p is less than 5. The point of the symbol is toward p, the lesser side.

items.q: What does x < 4 mean?
c: x is greater than or equal to 4
x is less than or equal to 4
items.e: Read from left to right: x is less than 4. The point of the symbol is toward x, the lesser side.

items.q: Which sentence means the same as 20 ≥ k?
c: k is less than or equal to 20
k is greater than or equal to 20
items.e: 20 ≥ k is read “20 is greater than or equal to k.” That means k is less than or equal to 20.

items.q: Which inequality means “t is greater than or equal to 25”?
items.e: “t is greater than or equal to 25” is written t ≥ 25, with t first. 25 ≥ t says “25 is greater than or equal to t,” which is the opposite.

items.q: What does y > 40 mean?
c: y is less than or equal to 40
y is greater than or equal to 40
items.e: Read from left to right: y is greater than 40. The symbol opens toward y, the greater side.

items.q: Which inequality means the same as 18 ≥ p?
items.e: 18 ≥ p says “18 is greater than or equal to p.” Turn it around: p is less than or equal to 18, so p ≤ 18. The symbol still opens toward the greater side.

items.q: Which sentence means the same as 7 > p?
c: p is less than or equal to 7
p is greater than or equal to 7
items.e: 7 > p is read “7 is greater than p.” That means p is less than 7.

items.q: Which inequality means “x is greater than 10”?
items.e: “x is greater than 10” is written x > 10, with x first. 10 > x says “10 is greater than x,” which is the opposite.

items.q: Which inequality means “k is greater than 27”?
items.e: “k is greater than 27” is written k > 27, with k first. 27 > k says “27 is greater than k,” which is the opposite.

items.q: Which sentence means the same as 29 < n?
c: n is greater than or equal to 29
n is less than or equal to 29
items.e: 29 < n is read “29 is less than n.” That means n is greater than 29.

items.q: Which number is a solution of x ≤ 15?
items.e: Test each number in x ≤ 15: 15 ≤ 15 is true; 16 ≤ 15 is false; 15 12 ≤ 15 is false; 20 ≤ 15 is false. Only 15 makes it true. ≥ and ≤ include the number itself.

items.q: Is 4 a solution of r < 4?
c: Yes, because 4 is the number in the inequality
No, because only numbers greater than 4 are solutions
No, because 4 is not less than 4
items.e: 4 < 4 is false. The sign has no “or equal to,” so 4 is left out.

items.q: Which number is a solution of p > 9?
items.e: Test each number in p > 9: 9 12 > 9 is true; 9 > 9 is false; 8 > 9 is false; 3 > 9 is false. Only 9 12 makes it true. 9 is not a solution, because 9 is not greater than itself.

items.q: Which list has only solutions of w < 0?
items.e: Every number in −1, −0.5, −8 makes w < 0 true. Each other list has a number that does not work: 0 in −1, 0, −3; 2 in −4, −2, 2; 0.5 in −5, −1, 0.5.

items.q: Which number is a solution of t > 2 12?
items.e: Test each number in t > 2 12: 3 > 2 12 is true; 2 12 > 2 12 is false; 2 > 2 12 is false; 1 12 > 2 12 is false. Only 3 makes it true. 2 12 is not a solution, because 2 12 is not greater than itself.

items.q: Which list has only solutions of t ≤ 4?
items.e: Every number in 1, 3, 4 makes t ≤ 4 true. Each other list has a number that does not work: 5 in 1, 3, 5; 6 in 4, 6, 8; 9 in 0, 2, 9.

items.q: Which number is not a solution of z ≥ 8?
items.e: Test each number in z ≥ 8: 7 12 ≥ 8 is false; 8 ≥ 8 is true; 8 12 ≥ 8 is true; 30 ≥ 8 is true. 7 12 is the only one that makes it false.

items.q: How many solutions does x > 3 have?
items.e: Every number greater than 3 works: 4, 3.5, 3.01, 100, 1,000,000 and so on. There is no end, so there are infinitely many solutions.

items.q: Is 20 a solution of t ≥ 20?
c: No, the circle at 20 is open
Yes, because every number is a solution
No, because 20 is not greater than 20
items.e: 20 ≥ 20 is true. The line under the sign means “or equal to,” so 20 is included.

items.q: How many solutions does y < 10 have?
items.e: Not just whole numbers work. 9.5, 2.25, 0 and −40 are also less than 10. There is no end, so there are infinitely many solutions.

items.q: Which number is a solution of m > −2?
items.e: Test each number in m > −2: 0 > −2 is true; −2 > −2 is false; −5 > −2 is false; −3 > −2 is false. Only 0 makes it true. −2 is not a solution, because −2 is not greater than itself. On a number line, −5 is to the left of −2, so −5 < −2.

items.q: Is 11 a solution of m ≤ 11?
c: Yes, because every number is a solution
No, the circle at 11 is open
No, because 11 is not less than 11
items.e: 11 ≤ 11 is true. The line under the sign means “or equal to,” so 11 is included.

items.q: Is 7 a solution of x > 7?
c: No, because only numbers less than 7 are solutions
No, because 7 is not greater than 7
Yes, because 7 is the number in the inequality
items.e: 7 > 7 is false. The sign has no “or equal to,” so 7 is left out.

items.q: Which number is a solution of y ≥ 12?
items.e: Test each number in y ≥ 12: 12 ≥ 12 is true; 11 ≥ 12 is false; 11 12 ≥ 12 is false; 2 ≥ 12 is false. Only 12 makes it true. ≥ and ≤ include the number itself.

items.q: Which number is not a solution of x ≤ −3?
items.e: Test each number in x ≤ −3: −2 ≤ −3 is false; −3 ≤ −3 is true; −4 ≤ −3 is true; −10 ≤ −3 is true. −2 is the only one that makes it false.

items.q: Which list has only solutions of k > 6?
items.e: Every number in 6.5, 7, 10 makes k > 6 true. Each other list has a number that does not work: 6 in 6, 7, 10; 2 in 2, 4, 8; 5 in 5, 6.5, 9.

items.q: Which number is a solution of n < 7?
items.e: Test each number in n < 7: 6.9 < 7 is true; 7 < 7 is false; 7.1 < 7 is false; 8 < 7 is false. Only 6.9 makes it true. 7 is not a solution, because 7 is not less than itself.

items.q: Which number is not a solution of w < 10?
items.e: Test each number in w < 10: 10 < 10 is false; 9.9 < 10 is true; 9 < 10 is true; 0 < 10 is true. 10 is the only one that makes it false. The number itself is not a solution of w < 10.

items.q: Which number is a solution of r < −4?
items.e: Test each number in r < −4: −6 < −4 is true; −4 < −4 is false; −2 < −4 is false; 0 < −4 is false. Only −6 makes it true. −4 is not a solution, because −4 is not less than itself. On a number line, −6 is to the left of −4, so −6 < −4.

items.q: Which number is not a solution of k > 5?
items.e: Test each number in k > 5: 5 > 5 is false; 5.1 > 5 is true; 6 > 5 is true; 20 > 5 is true. 5 is the only one that makes it false. The number itself is not a solution of k > 5.

sets.title: Graph inequalities on a number line

items.q: Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The circle is at 16. The circle is open, so 16 is not included, and the arrow points left (lesser numbers), so the inequality is x < 16.

items.q: Which number is a solution shown by the graph?
items.e: The graph shows x ≥ −1. Test each number in x ≥ −1: −1 ≥ −1 is true; −2 ≥ −1 is false; −4 ≥ −1 is false; −1.5 ≥ −1 is false. The closed circle means −1 is included.

items.q: Grace graphed x ≤ −4 like this. What is wrong?
c: The arrow should point the other way
The circle should be closed (filled in)
items.e: x ≤ −4 has a closed (filled-in) circle, because −4 itself is a solution, and the arrow points left, toward lesser numbers. Grace’s graph shows x < −4 instead.

items.q: Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The circle is at 1. The circle is closed, so 1 is included, and the arrow points left (lesser numbers), so the inequality is x ≤ 1.

items.q: Which number is a solution shown by the graph?
items.e: The graph shows x < 5. Test each number in x < 5: 2 < 5 is true; 5 < 5 is false; 6 < 5 is false; 9 < 5 is false. The open circle means 5 is not included.

items.q: Zoe graphed x > 10 like this. What is wrong?
c: The circle should be closed (filled in)
The arrow should point to the right
items.e: x > 10 has an open circle, because 10 itself is not a solution, and the arrow points right, toward greater numbers. Zoe’s graph shows x < 10 instead.

items.q: Which describes the graph of x ≥ 25 on a number line?
c: Closed circle at 25, shaded to the left
Open circle at 25, shaded to the left
Open circle at 25, shaded to the right
Closed circle at 25, shaded to the right
items.e: x ≥ 25 has a closed (filled-in) circle, because 25 itself is a solution, and the arrow points right, toward greater numbers.

items.q: Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The circle is at 4. The circle is open, so 4 is not included, and the arrow points right (greater numbers), so the inequality is x > 4.

items.q: Which describes the graph of x > 8 on a number line?
c: Open circle at 8, shaded to the left
Open circle at 8, shaded to the right
Closed circle at 8, shaded to the right
Closed circle at 8, shaded to the left
items.e: x > 8 has an open circle, because 8 itself is not a solution, and the arrow points right, toward greater numbers.

items.q: Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The circle is at 7. The circle is closed, so 7 is included, and the arrow points right (greater numbers), so the inequality is x ≥ 7.

items.q: Owen graphed x < 6 like this. What is wrong?
c: The circle should be closed (filled in)
The arrow should point to the left
items.e: x < 6 has an open circle, because 6 itself is not a solution, and the arrow points left, toward lesser numbers. Owen’s graph shows x > 6 instead.

items.q: Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The circle is at 0. The circle is closed, so 0 is included, and the arrow points right (greater numbers), so the inequality is x ≥ 0.

items.q: Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The circle is at −3. The circle is closed, so −3 is included, and the arrow points right (greater numbers), so the inequality is x ≥ −3.

items.q: Which describes the graph of x < −1 on a number line?
c: Open circle at −1, shaded to the right
Closed circle at −1, shaded to the right
Open circle at −1, shaded to the left
Closed circle at −1, shaded to the left
items.e: x < −1 has an open circle, because −1 itself is not a solution, and the arrow points left, toward lesser numbers.

items.q: Which describes the graph of x ≤ 3 on a number line?
c: Closed circle at 3, shaded to the left
Closed circle at 3, shaded to the right
Open circle at 3, shaded to the left
Open circle at 3, shaded to the right
items.e: x ≤ 3 has a closed (filled-in) circle, because 3 itself is a solution, and the arrow points left, toward lesser numbers.

items.q: Sam graphed x ≥ 2 like this. What is wrong?
c: The arrow should point the other way
The circle should be closed (filled in)
items.e: x ≥ 2 has a closed (filled-in) circle, because 2 itself is a solution, and the arrow points right, toward greater numbers. Sam’s graph shows x > 2 instead.

items.q: Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The circle is at 12. The circle is closed, so 12 is included, and the arrow points left (lesser numbers), so the inequality is x ≤ 12.

items.q: Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The circle is at −5. The circle is open, so −5 is not included, and the arrow points right (greater numbers), so the inequality is x > −5.

items.q: Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The circle is at −2. The circle is open, so −2 is not included, and the arrow points left (lesser numbers), so the inequality is x < −2.

items.q: Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The circle is at 9. The circle is open, so 9 is not included, and the arrow points left (lesser numbers), so the inequality is x < 9.

items.q: Which inequality shows “k is at most 3”?
items.e: “At most 3” means 3 or less, so use ≤. The inequality is k ≤ 3.

items.q: Which phrase means p < 23?
items.e: p < 23 means p is less than 23. “Less than” leaves the number out.

items.q: Which phrase means k ≤ 40?
items.e: k ≤ 40 means k is less than or equal to 40. “At most” means that number or less.

items.q: Which inequality shows “m is over 43”?
items.e: “Over 43” does not include 43, so use >. The inequality is m > 43.

items.q: Which inequality shows “p is at least 25”?
items.e: “At least 25” means 25 or more, so use ≥. The inequality is p ≥ 25.

items.q: Which inequality shows “the minimum value of z is 46”?
items.e: The minimum is the least value allowed, so z can be 46 or more: z ≥ 46.

items.q: Which inequality shows “m is 59 or more”?
items.e: “Or more” includes the number, so m can be 59 or greater: m ≥ 59.

items.q: Which phrase means r ≥ 45?
items.e: r ≥ 45 means r is greater than or equal to 45. “At least” means that number or more.

items.q: Which inequality shows “the maximum value of t is 19”?
items.e: The maximum is the greatest value allowed, so t can be 19 or less: t ≤ 19.

items.q: Which phrase means x > 29?
items.e: x > 29 means x is greater than 29. “More than” leaves the number out.

items.q: Which phrase means y ≤ 42?
items.e: y ≤ 42 means y is less than or equal to 42. “At most” means that number or less.

items.q: Which inequality shows “x is no less than 38”?
items.e: “No less than 38” means 38 or more, so use ≥. The inequality is x ≥ 38.

items.q: Which inequality shows “w is below 53”?
items.e: “Below 53” does not include 53, so use <. The inequality is w < 53.

items.q: Which inequality shows “y is under 56”?
items.e: “Under 56” does not include 56, so use <. The inequality is y < 56.

items.q: Which inequality shows “z is more than 51”?
items.e: “More than 51” does not include 51, so use >. The inequality is z > 51.

items.q: Which inequality shows “r is no more than 60”?
items.e: “No more than 60” means 60 or less, so use ≤. The inequality is r ≤ 60.

items.q: Which inequality shows “n is less than 8”?
items.e: “Less than 8” does not include 8, so use <. The inequality is n < 8.

items.q: Which inequality shows “t is greater than 32”?
items.e: “Greater than 32” does not include 32, so use >. The inequality is t > 32.

items.q: Which inequality shows “n is 31 or fewer”?
items.e: “Or fewer” includes the number, so n can be 31 or less: n ≤ 31.

items.q: Which phrase means w ≥ 26?
items.e: w ≥ 26 means w is greater than or equal to 26. “At least” means that number or more.

items.q: Which rule could this graph show? (x is age in years.)
c: You must be under 8 years old
You must be over 8 years old
You can be at most 8 years old
You must be at least 8 years old
items.e: The closed circle at 8 means 8 is included, and the arrow points right. That is x ≥ 8: 8 or older, which is “at least 8.” “Over 8” would need an open circle.

items.q: Sofia has $25 to spend on a gift. Let c be the cost of the gift in dollars. Which inequality shows the costs she can pay?
items.e: Sofia can spend all $25 or less, so the cost is at most 25: c ≤ 25.

items.q: To ride a roller coaster, you must be at least 44 inches tall. Let h be a rider’s height in inches. Which inequality shows the heights that can ride?
items.e: “At least 44” means 44 inches or taller. A rider who is exactly 44 inches can ride, so use ≥: h ≥ 44.

items.q: A water slide says: “Riders must be at least 42 inches tall.” Four friends measured their heights. Which height is allowed on the slide?
items.e: The heights allowed are h ≥ 42. 42 is equal to 42, and ≥ includes equal, so it is allowed. The others are less than 42.

items.q: Leo’s plant is taller than 22 centimeters. Which could be the height of the plant?
items.e: “Taller than 22” means h > 22. Only 22.5 is greater than 22. A plant that is exactly 22 cm is not taller than 22 cm.

items.q: Water freezes when the temperature is below 32°F. Let t be the temperature in °F. How many temperatures are solutions of t < 32?
c: Only the whole numbers from 0 to 31
items.e: Any temperature less than 32 works: 31.9, 20, 0, −5 and so on. Temperatures do not have to be whole numbers, and there is no end, so there are infinitely many solutions.

items.q: A field trip will happen only if at least 24 students sign up. Let s be the number of students who sign up. Which inequality shows when the trip will happen?
items.e: “At least 24” means 24 or more. A common mistake is to use ≤ or < because of the word “least.” The answer is s ≥ 24.

items.q: Which sentence could this graph show? (x is the temperature in °F.)
items.e: The open circle at 5 means 5 is not included, and the arrow points left. That is x < 5, “below 5.” “At most 5” would need a closed circle.

items.q: The speed limit on a road is 55 miles per hour. The legal speeds are s ≤ 55. Which speed is not allowed?
items.e: 57 > 55, so 57 mph is over the limit. 55 mph is exactly the limit, and ≤ includes it.

items.q: At a restaurant, kids under 12 eat free. Let a be a child’s age in years. Which inequality shows the ages that eat free?
items.e: “Under 12” means less than 12. A child who is 12 does not eat free, so use <, not ≤: a < 12.

items.q: To win a prize, you need a score of more than 80 points. Scores are whole numbers. What is the least score that wins?
items.e: “More than 80” means s > 80, so 80 does not win. The next whole number is 81. (90 also wins, but it is not the least.)

items.q: In a school zone, cars must drive no faster than 25 mph. Which describes the graph of the speeds s ≤ 25?
c: Closed circle at 25, shaded to the right
Open circle at 25, shaded to the left
Closed circle at 25, shaded to the left
Open circle at 25, shaded to the right
items.e: s ≤ 25 has a closed (filled-in) circle, because 25 itself is a solution, and the arrow points left, toward lesser numbers.

items.q: A soccer league needs a minimum of 11 players on each team. Noah writes p ≤ 11. Which is right?
c: p < 11, because the team must be smaller
p ≤ 11 is right, because a minimum is a small number
p ≥ 11, because a minimum of 11 means 11 or more
p > 11, because the minimum is not included
items.e: A minimum is the least number allowed. A team can have 11 players or more, so p ≥ 11.

items.q: A recipe says to bake the bread for at least 25 minutes. Let t be the baking time in minutes. Which inequality shows the baking times?
items.e: “At least 25 minutes” means 25 minutes or longer: t ≥ 25.

items.q: A class has fewer than 25 students. What is the greatest number of students the class could have?
items.e: “Fewer than 25” means s < 25, so 25 is not allowed. Students come in whole numbers, so the greatest is 24. (24.5 students makes no sense.)

items.q: A sign in an elevator says: “No more than 12 people.” Let p be the number of people. Which numbers make sense as solutions?
c: Every number less than or equal to 12
items.e: p ≤ 12, but you cannot have 3.5 or −2 people. Only whole numbers make sense, and 12 is allowed, so the solutions are 0, 1, 2, … , 12.

items.q: Ava says x > 3 has only 4 solutions: 4, 5, 6 and 7. Is she right?
c: No. Every number greater than 3 works, so there are infinitely many
Yes. Those are all the solutions
items.e: 8, 3.5, 100 and 1,000 are also greater than 3. The solutions never end, so x > 3 has infinitely many solutions. 3 is not one of them.

items.q: An elevator can carry a maximum of 2,000 pounds. Let w be the weight it carries in pounds. Which inequality shows the weights it can carry?
items.e: The maximum is the greatest weight allowed, and 2,000 pounds itself is allowed: w ≤ 2,000.

items.q: An airline says a checked bag can weigh at most 40 pounds. Which bag weight is allowed?
items.e: “At most 40” means w ≤ 40. 40 = 40, so a 40-pound bag is allowed. The others are more than 40.

items.q: A phone plan lets you use no more than 5 GB of data each month. Let d be the data used in GB. Which inequality matches the plan?
items.e: “No more than 5” means 5 or less, and 5 is allowed: d ≤ 5.
